Title: Boots on the Moon
Content: Many of us have gazed at the moon. The moon is about `text(239,000 miles)` away from `text(Earth)`. Most of us will never get there. But some people have really stood on the moon and gazed back at `text(Earth)`. These space travelers were astronauts who took part in missions to explore the moon

During the `text(1960s)`, the United States of America was in a race with other countries to put the `text(first)` astronaut on the moon. The goal was to land people on the moon and bring them safely back to `text(Earth)`. That is how the Apollo Program, also known as Project Apollo, began.

The Apollo Program ran from `1961` to `1972`. The program had many missions. Only `12` of those missions sent people to space. Most of the early missions only orbited the moon. By the `text(year 1969)`, no one had landed on the moon. But that was all about to change.

Apollo `11`, the `text(sixth)` mission with people, was the `text(first)` to land on the moon. The flight crew consisted of `text(three)` astronauts: Commander Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins. For `text(months)`, the astronauts practiced and prepared. On `text(July 16, 1969)`, they were ready. Apollo `11` blasted off from Kennedy Space Center. More than `text(600 million)` people watched the `ultext(launch)` on their televisions. They cheered for the history-making moment.

Apollo `11` landed on the moon on `text(July 20)`. Armstrong was the `text(first)` astronaut to `ultext(emerge)` from the spacecraft. As he stepped onto the moon's surface, he said, “That's `text(one)` small step for a man, `text(one)` giant leap for mankind.”

During this mission, Armstrong and Aldrin explored the moon for `text(2 hours and 32 minutes)`. They collected samples, conducted experiments, and took photographs. They used special tools designed for their mission. Because their spacesuits were bulky, it was difficult for the astronauts to move and bend. Special rakes, scoops, hammers, and tubes had long handles that allowed the astronauts to collect rocks and soil without bending.

Apollo `11` carried the `text(first)` rock samples back to `text(Earth)`, but the astronauts left some things on the moon too. They left an American flag, an arm patch from Apollo `1`, and a metal sign with a message on it. Apollo `11` returned to `text(Earth)` on `text(July 24, 1969)`.
Between `1969` and `1972`, America launched `text(five)` more Apollo missions. During those missions, `text(eight)` more astronauts put their boots on the moon.
`text(One)` mission, Apollo `13`, was not able to land on the moon because of an emergency. The astronauts and spacecraft were brought safely back to `text(Earth)`.

Apollo `17`, the final mission, lifted off on `text(December 7, 1972)`. It was the `text(first)` nighttime liftoff in the history of American space travel. The `text(three-person)` crew included Commander Eugene Cernan, Harrison Schmitt, and Ronald Evans.

Apollo `17` landed on the moon on `text(December 11)`. Cernan and Schmitt climbed out of the spacecraft. When Schmitt's feet hit the ground, he became the `text(first)` geologist, or rock scientist, to put boots on the moon.

Cernan and Schmitt spent a total of `text(74 hours)`, `text(59 minutes)`, and `text(40 seconds)` on the moon. They had a tool that had never been used before-a battery-powered vehicle. The vehicle could carry `text(two)` astronauts, tools, equipment, and samples. The `text(two)` astronauts traveled almost `text(22 miles)` across the moon's surface. They brought back more samples than any of the other Apollo missions.

Apollo `17` left the moon on `text(December 14)`. As Cernan's boots left the surface, he said, “As we leave the `text(Moon)` ... we leave as we came ... with peace and hope for all mankind.” The astronauts returned to `text(Earth)` on `text(December 19, 1972)`.

All together, the Apollo missions brought back `text(842 pounds)` of materials from the moon's surface. Astronauts collected rocks, pebbles, dirt, sand, and dust from `text(six)` different places on the moon. These samples helped scientists understand how the solar system formed. Even now, many `text(years)` later, moon samples are still being shared with scientists and teachers. The Apollo program may have ended, but its discoveries continue to teach us about space.
